reason: The story focuses on elite figures and patriarchs rather than working people. The main characters are Shechem (נְשִׂיא הָאָרֶץ, 'prince of the land'), his father Hamor (a city ruler), and Jacob (a wealthy patriarch). The narrative employs an omniscient third-person perspective centered on negotiations and actions of these ruling-class figures. While the text mentions 'the men of the city' (אַנְשֵׁי עִירָם) as participants, they appear only as followers of their leaders' directives, not as the narrative perspective. The entire account concerns itself with the concerns of the aristocratic classes—marriage alliances, family honor, and matters of rulership—rather than the perspectives or concerns of working people.
